lead: Many images hold two things: something bright and something dark. Thresholding turns such an image into black and white by comparing every pixel with a single grey level T. It is the cheapest segmentation method — one comparison per pixel — and the first thing to try on scanned documents, parts on an inspection line, cells on a slide and CT slices. The hard part is choosing T. Otsu's method searches the histogram for the split that pushes the two classes farthest apart.
prereq: Unit 1 histograms and Unit 2 histogram processing; Otsu's search runs on the histogram alone.

sections.h3: From grey image to binary image

blocks.text: Thresholding compares every pixel with one number T, the threshold, and outputs a binary image. Pixels above T become 1 (foreground), the rest 0. It is a point operation: it never looks at a neighbour.
g(x, y) = 1 if f(x, y) > T, else g(x, y) = 0
blocks.where: f(x, y) is the input grey level (0 to 255 for 8-bit); T is a grey level, not a pixel count; g(x, y) is the binary output.

blocks.text: The method exists because many scenes contain exactly two materials. On the histogram such an image is bimodal: one peak for the background, one for the object, and a valley between them. The valley is the natural T.

Light is the hidden assumption. A camera records f(x, y) = i(x, y) · r(x, y), where i is illumination and r is reflectance (0 to 1). Illumination does not change the object, but it shifts grey levels: a page lit from one corner is darker at the far corner, and one global T cuts paper as ink or loses part of a letter.

Uses: document binarisation before OCR, defect checks on a conveyor, counting stained cells, separating bone from soft tissue in a CT slice, and producing a mask for later steps such as region growing.

sections.h3: Basic global thresholding: iterate on the mean

blocks.text: When the valley is not obvious, an older iterative procedure finds T from the two class means.

items: Set T to the mean grey level of the whole image.
Split with T: pixels with f ≤ T go to G1, pixels with f > T go to G2.
Compute μ1 and μ2, the means of G1 and G2.
Repeat steps 2 to 4 until T changes by less than ΔT, often 1 grey level or 0.

blocks.text: Each pass pulls T towards the midpoint between the class means, roughly the valley. A clean bimodal image settles in a few passes. It is a heuristic, not an optimum: three peaks can lock it onto the wrong valley, and it still uses one T for the whole image.

sections.h3: Otsu's method: maximise the between-class variance

blocks.text: Otsu asks: which k makes the two classes cleanest? Build the normalised histogram p(i) = h(i)/(MN), where h(i) counts pixels at grey level i and MN is the pixel count. For candidate k, class 0 is levels 0 to k and class 1 is levels k+1 to L−1, with L = 256.

items: w0(k) = Σ p(i) for i = 0 to k, the fraction of pixels in class 0; w1(k) = 1 − w0(k).
μ0(k) = [Σ i · p(i) for i = 0 to k] / w0(k), the mean grey level of class 0; μ1(k) is the same sum over levels k+1 to L−1 divided by w1(k).

blocks.where: σB²(k) is the between-class variance in grey levels squared; w0, w1 are class fractions; μ0, μ1 are class means. The best threshold k* maximises σB²(k).

blocks.text: Search k from 0 to L−2, keep the largest σB², and set T = k*. Pixels with f ≤ k* become 0; pixels with f > k* become 1. The split rule matters: writing level k on the wrong side changes the binary image even when σB² is the same.

Within-class form: σW² = w0σ0² + w1σ1², and σT² = σW² + σB². σT² is fixed for a histogram, so minimising σW² gives the same k. One pass over L = 256 bins costs O(L) time and memory; after the histogram is built, the image is never touched again.

sections.h3: When one T is not enough

blocks.text: Otsu is global: it assumes a bimodal histogram and two classes of comparable size. Three common failures: one class covers a tiny part of the image, so the split barely changes w0 and w1; the histogram is unimodal, so the best split falls in a tail; illumination varies, so the same material gives two grey levels in two places.

The cheap fix is variable thresholding: split the image into blocks, say 32 × 32, run Otsu inside each, and interpolate the per-block thresholds across boundaries. A shadow is then handled locally instead of dragging the whole threshold with it.

figure.caption: For counts 4, 6, 6, 4 the between-class variance is 0.5625, 0.81 and 0.5625 at k = 0, 1, 2. It peaks at k = 1, so T = 1 puts levels 0 and 1 in one class and 2 and 3 in the other.

examples.question: A 20-pixel image has four grey levels with histogram counts h(0) = 4, h(1) = 6, h(2) = 6, h(3) = 4. Use Otsu's method to find the threshold, and state which grey levels fall in each class.
steps: The largest value is 0.81 at k = 1, so T = 1. Class 0 holds levels 0 and 1 (10 pixels); class 1 holds levels 2 and 3 (10 pixels).
examples.answer: The Otsu threshold is T = 1: grey levels 0 and 1 become 0, and grey levels 2 and 3 become 1.
examples.check:
h = [4, 6, 6, 4]
N = sum(h)
p = [c / N for c in h]
print(round(sum(i * p[i] for i in range(4)), 4))
sb = []
for k in range(3):
    w0 = sum(p[:k + 1])
    w1 = 1 - w0
    m0 = sum(i * p[i] for i in range(k + 1)) / w0
    m1 = sum(i * p[i] for i in range(k + 1, 4)) / w1
    v = w0 * w1 * (m0 - m1) ** 2
    sb.append(v)
    print(round(v, 4))
print(sb.index(max(sb)))

traps: Otsu maximises σB². If you work with σW² you must minimise it; writing maximise σW² loses marks.

Fix the split rule and say it: level ≤ k is class 0. If two k values tie at the maximum σB², pick one by your rule, keep it fixed and state it. In the worked example there is no tie: 0.81 at k = 1 beats 0.5625 at k = 0 and k = 2.
Otsu is an exhaustive search over k on the histogram, not an iterative mean-splitting loop. That loop is a different, older method.
Thresholding cannot remove noise, because it ignores neighbours. A single bright noisy pixel above T becomes foreground; filter first, then threshold.

quiz.q: Write the thresholding rule for g(x, y) in terms of f(x, y) and T, and define each symbol.
quiz.a: g(x, y) = 1 if f(x, y) > T, else 0. f is the input grey level, T is the chosen grey-level threshold, g is the binary output.

quiz.q: Why does uneven illumination break a single global threshold?
quiz.a: The camera records f = i · r, so illumination multiplies reflectance. The same surface then gives different grey levels in lit and shaded parts; one T is correct in one region and wrong in the other.

quiz.q: A 10-pixel image has histogram counts h = [2, 2, 4, 2] on levels 0 to 3. Compute σB² for k = 0, 1, 2 and give the Otsu threshold.
A histogram has one tall peak at grey level 40 and a long flat tail up to 255, and Otsu returns k = 120. Explain why this threshold may be poor.
quiz.a: The histogram is not bimodal. Otsu maximises σB² = w0w1(μ0 − μ1)², so it rewards two well separated, compact, balanced classes. A single tall peak with a long tail has no second compact cluster, so the best k slides into the tail: every tail pixel above k = 120 becomes foreground, so noise and edge pixels become objects, while a real object near the peak is lost into the background.

quiz.q: Show that maximising σB² is the same as minimising σW².
quiz.a: σT² = σW² + σB², and σT² is the variance of the whole image, fixed for a given histogram. So the largest σB² occurs exactly where σW² is smallest.

quiz.q: What do w0(k) and μ0(k) mean in Otsu's formula?
quiz.a: w0(k) is the fraction of pixels whose grey level is at most k (class 0); μ0(k) is the mean grey level of those pixels.

beyond: Not for the exam. Otsu ships in every vision library (OpenCV's THRESH_OTSU, scikit-image's threshold_otsu) and remains the first pass in industrial inspection. Two-dimensional Otsu builds a joint histogram of grey level and neighbourhood mean to resist noise. Multi-level Otsu extends the between-class variance to three or more classes with a search over two thresholds. Local methods such as Sauvola and Niblack compute a fresh T from each pixel's neighbourhood. Search for 2D Otsu, multi-level Otsu and Sauvola thresholding to go further.
